title: august
description: A hazy, sun-drenched daydream of a summer romance that was never really hers, told by the girl on the other side of folklore's teenage love triangle. The official lyric video drifts over swaying beach grass as August slips away like a bottle of wine.

pops.text: Swift wrote 'august' with Jack Antonoff; the pair produced it with Joe Alwyn.
It is track 8 on folklore, Swift's surprise eighth album, released July 24, 2020.
The song opens with salt air and the rust on a door — pure seaside summer.
It is one third of folklore's 'Teenage Love Triangle,' alongside 'cardigan' and 'betty.'
The narrator — fans call her Augustine — sings about James, who was never hers to lose.
Swift wrote 'august' first of the three triangle songs.
She imagined the story as fiction, a shift from her usual autobiographical writing.
The chorus turns the month into a drink: August 'sipped away like a bottle of wine.'
folklore was written and recorded remotely during the COVID-19 lockdown months.
Every August 1st, fans flood social media with the song as summer nostalgia peaks.

title: Prince Caspian
description: Phish close Billy Breathes by floating out to sea with C.S. Lewis's Prince Caspian, all shimmering guitars and a chorus that keeps rising like waves. In concert it became a launchpad for long, soaring jams.

pops.text: The song is named for Prince Caspian of C.S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia.
Lyrics are by Tom Marshall, Trey Anastasio's longtime songwriting partner.
It is the closing track — number 13 — on 1996's Billy Breathes.
Billy Breathes was produced by Steve Lillywhite, famed for work with U2 and Peter Gabriel.
Phish debuted the song live in 1995, a year before the album arrived.
The studio version runs about five minutes; live versions often stretch far beyond.
On Billy Breathes it follows the quiet title track, ending the album on an oceanic swell.
Fans often shorten its name to just 'Caspian' on setlists.
Its two-chord vamp made it a favorite mid-set breather that can suddenly take flight.
At Magnaball in 2015 a celebrated late-night 'Caspian' reminded fans how big it can grow.

title: Disturbance at the Heron House
description: A jangling Peter Buck riff carries Michael Stipe's animal fable of a revolution caged and quieted, tucked into Document, the album that broke R.E.M. into the mainstream. Pretty on the surface, pointed underneath.

pops.text: Stipe said the song was his take on George Orwell's Animal Farm.
He aimed Orwell's failed-revolution allegory at Ronald Reagan's America.
It is track 4 on Document, R.E.M.'s fifth studio album, released in 1987.
Document was the band's last album for the indie label I.R.S. Records.
It was co-produced by Scott Litt, beginning a long R.E.M.–Litt partnership.
Fans noted 'Heron House' echoes 'Herrenhaus,' German for a lord's mansion.
The recording was made at Sound Emporium in Nashville in spring 1987.
Document became R.E.M.'s first platinum album and first US Top 10 record.
R.E.M. revived the song acoustically for MTV Unplugged and Mountain Stage in 1991.
Mike Mills's harmony vocals shadow Stipe through the choruses.

title: Loving Cup
description: Nicky Hopkins's grand piano opens one of the Stones' most tender songs, a gospel-tinged toast that closes side two of Exile on Main St. Mick and Keith harmonize like a barroom choir asking for one little drink.

pops.text: An early version was recorded in 1969 during the Let It Bleed sessions at Olympic Studios.
The band played it at Hyde Park on July 5, 1969, as 'Gimme a Little Drink.'
That Hyde Park show was Mick Taylor's debut and came two days after Brian Jones's death.
The Exile version was finished at Sunset Sound in Los Angeles in late 1971 into 1972.
Nicky Hopkins's piano is the song's beating heart, from intro to fade.
Bobby Keys on sax and Jim Price on horns give the ending its gospel lift.
Producer Jimmy Miller even joins in, playing percussion on the track.
Ex-manager Allen Klein sued over the song, claiming it dated from his ABKCO era — and won publishing rights.
It returned to setlists on the 2002–03 Licks Tour after years away.
Jack White joined the Stones for 'Loving Cup' in the 2008 concert film Shine a Light.

title: Get Off of My Cloud
description: Written under pressure to follow 'Satisfaction,' this stomping two-finger salute to fame and botheration topped the charts on both sides of the Atlantic. Charlie Watts's drum intro still kicks the door in.

pops.text: Jagger and Richards wrote it as the follow-up single to '(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction.'
It was recorded September 6–7, 1965 at RCA Studios in Hollywood.
Producer Andrew Loog Oldham rushed it out within weeks of the session.
It hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 for two weeks in November 1965.
It also spent three weeks at No. 1 in the UK.
The 'cloud' is Jagger's metaphor for his peace being crowded by hangers-on and demands.
Keith Richards later felt the recording was rushed and over-compressed for radio.
Brian Jones and Keith Richards supply the twin-guitar attack; Ian Stewart plays piano.
The US B-side was 'I'm Free,' later covered by the Soup Dragons.
In the US it appeared on the album December's Children (And Everybody's).

title: Disco
description: No mirror balls required: this wordless funk workout is Widespread Panic's four-on-the-floor dance party, built for JoJo Hermann's clavinet and a rhythm section that never lets up. This official Red Rocks performance shows why it has opened countless Panic shows.

pops.text: 'Disco' is an instrumental — not a mirror-ball cover or a Bee Gees tribute.
Widespread Panic debuted it on August 4, 1988 at the Uptown Lounge in Athens, Georgia.
Its name comes from the steady four-on-the-floor drum beat underneath.
It was shelved while keyboardist T. Lavitz was in the band, returning in March 1992.
JoJo Hermann's piano and clavinet are the song's lead voice.
It opened the famous Panic in the Streets show in Athens in 1998.
Panic have rarely gone more than a handful of shows without playing it.
It frequently segues straight into another song without a pause.
This video captures it live at Red Rocks Amphitheatre in Colorado in 2023.
Widespread Panic formed in Athens, Georgia, home of R.E.M. and the B-52's.

title: Octopus's Garden
description: Ringo Starr invites everyone under the sea in the Beatles' most beloved children's song, born from a boat captain's tale about octopuses building gardens of shiny stones. Bubbles, gurgles and sunshine included.

pops.text: Ringo wrote it after a 1968 boat trip in Sardinia aboard Peter Sellers's yacht.
He ordered fish and chips and was served squid for the first time: 'It tasted like chicken.'
The captain explained that octopuses collect stones and shiny objects to build gardens.
Ringo later said he also just wanted to hide under the sea amid band tensions.
George Harrison helped him finish the chords — you can see it in the Let It Be film.
It is one of only two songs Ringo wrote for the Beatles, after 'Don't Pass Me By.'
The band recorded 32 takes of the backing track in April 1969.
George made the bubble sounds by blowing through a straw into a glass of milk.
Paul and George's backing vocals were treated to sound like they're gurgling underwater.
It was never a single, yet became a favorite of generations of kids.

title: Colors of the Wind
description: Pocahontas teaches John Smith — and every kid watching — to listen with his heart in Disney's Oscar-winning anthem to nature and understanding. Judy Kuhn, Pocahontas's singing voice, delivers the film version heard in theaters.

pops.text: Music is by Alan Menken; lyrics are by Stephen Schwartz of Wicked fame.
Judy Kuhn was Pocahontas's singing voice; Irene Bedard spoke the dialogue.
It won the Academy Award for Best Original Song.
It also won the Golden Globe for Best Original Song and a Grammy Award.
Pocahontas was Disney's 33rd animated feature film, released in 1995.
The song asks listeners if they can 'sing with all the voices of the mountain.'
Schwartz drew on Native American imagery and his own love of nature for the lyric.
Vanessa Williams sang a pop version over the end credits — this is the film version.
The Pocahontas soundtrack album reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200.
In the film, the song's swirling leaves became one of Disney's iconic images.

title: Stay with Me
description: Rod Stewart and Ronnie Wood's raucous one-night-stand rocker from A Nod Is As Good As a Wink... to a Blind Horse — Faces' only major American hit and still their signature song.

pops.text: Ronnie Wood remembers the song being born in a dressing room in the US — he thinks Detroit — before a show. Stewart asked him to play something to get ready for the gig, Wood hit the chord sequence, and Stewart started improvising words over it.

The woman in the lyric has a name: 'I know your name is Rita, 'cause your perfume's smelling sweeter.' By the final verse the narrator has already forgotten it and asks, 'Hey, what's your name again?'
Faces were a supergroup in reverse: Small Faces survivors Ronnie Lane, Ian McLagan and Kenney Jones, joined by Stewart and Wood, both fresh from the Jeff Beck Group.
It's the first single from the band's third album, A Nod Is As Good As a Wink... to a Blind Horse (1971), produced by the band with Glyn Johns.
Stewart and Wood share the writing credit, and the record is pure Faces lineup: Stewart singing, Wood on guitar, Lane on bass, McLagan on keyboards and Jones on drums.
Released in December 1971, it climbed to No. 6 in the UK and No. 17 on the Billboard Hot 100 — and spent two weeks at No. 10 on the Cash Box chart.
That No. 17 made it Faces' only major hit in the United States, even though the band landed three more Top 20 singles back home in the UK.
Timing helped: Stewart's solo 'Maggie May' was conquering charts on both sides of the Atlantic just as Faces were finishing this album, so the world was waiting for more of that voice.
In 1993 Stewart reunited with Wood for MTV Unplugged and cut a live version for Unplugged... and Seated — the old dressing-room song, seated and acoustic.
The covers keep coming: Def Leppard on Yeah!, Train live in 2004, McFly as a B-side in 2007, and Mary J. Blige for The Umbrella Academy soundtrack in 2019.

title: One Nation Under a Groove
description: George Clinton's dance-as-freedom manifesto — the title track of Funkadelic's biggest album, six weeks at No. 1 on the R&B chart, and a permanent entry in funk's founding documents.

pops.text: George Clinton told The Guardian in 2018 that the title phrase came from two young fans, Darlene and LaTanya, in Washington, DC — 'Chocolate City.' He credited them on the album cover.

The writers are Clinton, Garry Shider and Walter 'Junie' Morrison. Morrison, freshly arrived from the Ohio Players, was new to Funkadelic — this album was his first with the band, and his synthesizers reshaped their sound.
Clinton has said the song could have been a Parliament record, but Funkadelic needed a hit — Parliament had just scored with 'Flash Light,' while Funkadelic had never had a Top 40 single.
The band recorded the album at United Sound Studios in Detroit, Clinton's P-Funk workshop of choice.
The lyric treats dancing as liberation: one nation, united not by a flag but by 'gettin' down just for the funk of it.'
Released in September 1978, the single spent six weeks at No. 1 on Billboard's R&B chart — the longest run of any No. 1 single released that year.
On the Hot 100 it peaked at No. 28, Funkadelic's only Top 40 hit there, and it became the band's first million-selling single.
In Britain it did even better proportionally: No. 9 in January 1979, and still the band's only UK hit single.
The parent album was Funkadelic's commercial peak — No. 16 on the Billboard 200, their only No. 1 R&B album, and their only platinum LP.

Legacy check: the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame put it on its list of 500 Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll, Rolling Stone ranked it among the greatest dance songs ever, and Ice Cube rebuilt it as 'Bop Gun (One Nation)' in 1994.

title: You Sexy Thing
description: Errol Brown's 'I believe in miracles' soul gem that started life as a B-side nobody believed in — then hit the UK Top 10 in three different decades.

pops.text: Lead singer Errol Brown co-wrote it with bassist Tony Wilson. Brown, born in Jamaica and raised in the UK, fronted a band he and Wilson had formed back in 1969.
Producer Mickie Most didn't believe in this miracle at all: he first buried the song as the B-side of the ballad 'Blue Night.'
Most changed his mind, had the band re-record it, and released it as an A-side on his RAK label in October 1975 — the version you're hearing.
It reached No. 2 on the UK Singles Chart in November 1975 and No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 the following February.
Billboard ranked it the No. 22 song of 1976 in the US — remarkable mileage for a record that began on a flip side.
The whole song hangs on one of pop's simplest hooks: 'I believe in miracles — where you from, you sexy thing?'
In 1987 a remix by Ben Liebrand took it back to No. 10 in the UK, and the compilation The Very Best of Hot Chocolate, built around that remix, reached No. 1 on the UK Albums Chart.
That made it, at the time, a chart freak: the only song to reach the UK Top 10 in the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s — the third visit was still to come.
In 1997 The Full Monty put it back at No. 6: Robert Carlyle's Gaz rehearses his striptease to it in one of the film's most quoted scenes.
The song never really leaves — films, ads and TV shows from The Office to Supernatural keep reintroducing Brown's warm, unhurried vocal to new generations.

title: She Caught the Katy and Left Me a Mule to Ride
description: Taj Mahal's joyful blues standard about a woman who took the fast train and left him the slow animal — later the opening-credits music of The Blues Brothers.

pops.text: Taj Mahal co-wrote it with James Rachell — better known as Yank Rachell, a veteran blues mandolin player from Tennessee who had been recording since the 1920s generation of bluesmen.
The 'Katy' is not a woman. It's a train: the Missouri-Kansas-Texas Railroad, nicknamed the Katy from its M-K-T initials and stock symbol, K-T.
That's the joke in the title — she caught a fast, modern train out of town, and all she left him for transport was a mule.
It first appeared on The Natch'l Blues (1968), Taj Mahal's second album, released the same year as his self-titled debut.
Taj Mahal is a stage name: he was born Henry Saint Clair Fredericks Jr. in Harlem in 1942 and grew up in a deeply musical household.
The 1968 recording is stacked with talent, including guitarist Jesse Ed Davis, pianist Al Kooper and drummer Earl Palmer.
The song is built like a train ride — a rolling, upbeat blues that turns being left behind into something almost celebratory.
In 1980 The Blues Brothers put the Blues Brothers Band's version over the film's opening credits, playing as Jake Blues walks out of prison.
According to John Belushi's widow Judith, it was Belushi's favorite blues song.

It has since become a true blues standard, covered many times over — and Gillian Welch even wove its lyric into her 2001 song 'Revelator.' The railroad itself is gone, its Missouri tracks now the Katy Trail.

title: Deadbeat Club
description: The B-52's wistful postcard from their Athens youth — hanging out in cafes, doing nothing beautifully — from the comeback triumph of Cosmic Thing.

pops.text: This was the first piece of music Keith Strickland composed for Cosmic Thing, and its autobiographical lyrics about the band's early Athens life became a blueprint for the whole album.
The song looks back at the band's early days in Athens, Georgia, hanging around cafes drinking coffee for hours.
Because they didn't work or do much of anything, their parents nicknamed them the 'deadbeat club' — the band turned the insult into a badge of honor.
The lyric name-checks real Athens geography, including Allen's Hamburgers and Normaltown, the neighborhood that produced both the B-52's and R.E.M.
All four members — Cindy Wilson, Kate Pierson, Fred Schneider and Strickland — share the writing credit, and Wilson and Pierson's harmonies carry the nostalgia.
Cosmic Thing was a comeback record: the band had been on hiatus after guitarist Ricky Wilson, Cindy's brother, died in 1985.
The album was produced by Nile Rodgers and Don Was; 'Deadbeat Club' is credited to Rodgers.
The video was shot on location in Athens and features a cameo by the town's other famous frontman — R.E.M.'s Michael Stipe, lounging on a sofa.
Released as the fifth and final single from Cosmic Thing, it reached No. 30 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1990.
The parent album climbed into the US Top 5 and went multi-platinum, powered by 'Love Shack' and 'Roam' — with this gentler song as its fond farewell.

title: What Have I Done to Deserve This?
description: Pet Shop Boys' elegant duet with Dusty Springfield — a song written years earlier, waiting for exactly her voice, that returned a 60s icon to No. 2 on both sides of the Atlantic.

pops.text: The song was co-written with American songwriter Allee Willis, and Neil Tennant and Chris Lowe demoed it around Christmas 1984 — years before it was released.
It was originally intended for their debut album Please, but it was held back for one reason: they couldn't decide who should sing the other half of the duet.
Various contemporary singers were suggested and rejected. Eventually the duo's manager's assistant suggested Dusty Springfield.
Tennant jumped at it — he has cited Dusty's Dusty in Memphis as one of his favourite albums, and her voice was the one he'd imagined.
Springfield hadn't had a major hit in years, but she accepted, sang on the record and appeared in its theatre-set promotional video alongside Tennant and Lowe in evening dress.
Released on 10 August 1987 as the second single from the duo's second album Actually, it was produced by Stephen Hague.
It peaked at No. 2 in both the UK and on the Billboard Hot 100, and went to No. 1 in Ireland and on Billboard's Dance Club Play chart.
For Springfield it was the biggest American hit of her entire career — her highest US showing since 'You Don't Have to Say You Love Me' in 1966.
The duo performed it with Springfield at the 1988 BRIT Awards, the comeback moment in front of the whole British music industry.
It reopened her career: Pet Shop Boys went on to write and produce 'Nothing Has Been Proved' and 'In Private' for her, and half of her 1990 album Reputation.

title: Under the Milky Way
description: Australian band the Church's shimmering signature song — 12-string guitar, a solo that sounds like bagpipes but isn't, and a title borrowed from an Amsterdam venue.

pops.text: Steve Kilbey, the band's bassist and singer, wrote it with his then-girlfriend Karin Jansson of the band Curious (Yellow).
According to the press release issued with Starfish, the title comes from the Melkweg in Amsterdam — Dutch for 'Milky Way' — a music and cultural venue Kilbey used to frequent.
The band travelled to Los Angeles in 1987 to record their fifth album, Starfish, with producers Waddy Wachtel and Greg Ladanyi.
The track is built on a 12-string acoustic guitar melody — unusually gentle for a band known for layered electric psychedelia.
That famous solo is not bagpipes: it was played with an EBow on a Fender Jazzmaster and recorded on a Synclavier, producing the bagpipe-like wail.
The drums took special handling — the band played the song to a click track, and session player Russ Kunkel was later brought in to add the drums and percussion.
Released as a single on 15 February 1988, with Starfish issued at the same time, it became the band's breakthrough far beyond Australia.
It peaked at No. 22 in Australia and reached the US Top 40 — the band's only international hit of that scale.
At the ARIA Music Awards of 1989 it won Single of the Year in the band's home country.

The band made two videos — one for the Australian launch and a second, more elaborate one for the American release — and the song found a new generation in 2001 on the Donnie Darko soundtrack. Kilbey calls it a 'portal': ambiguous enough to mean whatever the listener needs.
